intro: Day two of twenty-three: Old Cairo, where the group lands at dawn and walks down into a sunken Roman fortress. Matthew's flight to Egypt, read with the whole of Hosea 11 and Isaiah's blessing on Egypt, turns a refuge story into a promise about Egypt itself.

stories.headline: Old Cairo lies buried under six metres of itself
stories.dek: The Coptic quarter was a toll gate on a canal, the ground has risen several metres since the Romans, and the water now comes from below rather than from the flood.
body: The group's first site after a night without sleep is not a hilltop or a holy cave but a hinge. The Roman fortress of Babylon stood on the east bank of the Nile, at the point where Lower Egypt (the delta) met Middle Egypt (the valley), and where river traffic paid its tolls. It also guarded the mouth of the old canal that linked the Nile to the Red Sea, the waterway Darius re-dug and Trajan later rebuilt as the Amnis Traianus. That canal ran between two great round towers and straight through the fortress (Wikipedia's Babylon Fortress article, summarising the recent archaeology).

In other words, the place Coptic tradition chose for the Holy Family's refuge was a junction: a customs post, a harbour and a canal head on the main river road of Egypt. The Abu Sirga note covers the fortress as an irony of empire. This edition reads it as a piece of plumbing. Everything about Old Cairo's ground today, from its stairs to its damp crypts, follows from that original position beside moving water.
## A hinge between delta and valley

Stand anywhere in the quarter and the geography is still readable if you know what to look for. West, across a narrow arm of the Nile, lies Roda Island, which antiquity called the Babylonian Island after the fortress. North and east lie the mounds and streets of Fustat, the camp that the Arab army pitched beside the besieged fortress and that became Egypt's first Islamic capital. Behind them, the Mokattam escarpment rises on the eastern skyline; the group will be up there tomorrow at the Cave Church. The quarter sits on low ground between river and hills, which is exactly why a fort was put here and exactly why water has been its problem ever since.

The river itself has moved. The fortress was built to touch the water; today the Nile channel lies some distance to the west behind modern streets and the Corniche road. The exact distance of the shift varies by period and source, so treat any single figure you hear from a guide as approximate.
## The ground has risen

The most striking physical fact about Old Cairo is how far down the Roman city lies. The Wikipedia article on the Hanging Church notes that the land surface has risen roughly six metres since the Roman period, which is why the Roman tower beside it is mostly buried. The American Research Center in Egypt (ARCE), which monitored engineering works here, puts Roman street levels three to five metres under the modern city, and its monitored borings went down about ten metres.

The pilgrims will feel this with their knees. The way into the Coptic lanes is down a flight of steps from the modern street. Every step down is a step back toward the ground the Roman garrison walked on. It is worth saying so on the stairs: the city of Matthew's century is beneath your feet, not around you.
## Water from below

The Abu Sirga note mentions that the crypt regularly filled with water and reads that theologically. The mechanism today is not the Nile flood (which no longer comes; see Day 1) but groundwater. ARCE reports that by the late twentieth century the whole neighbourhood was endangered by high groundwater. USAID funded a groundwater-lowering project from 1999, and ARCE carried out archaeological monitoring alongside the engineers from 2000 to 2006. A USAID-captioned photograph of the works describes a series of collection and conveyance shafts drawing water away from St George's, the Mosque of Amr, the Roman tower, Abu Serga, Ben Ezra and the Hanging Church, completed in August 2006, which made the floors of flooded buildings accessible again.

So if the crypt at Abu Sirga is open and dry on 20 December, that dryness is itself an engineering story. If it is closed, damp or roped off, the reason is very likely the same water. Do not promise the group the crypt until the guide confirms on the morning.
## Late December in the lanes

The weather is the kindest of the whole trip. WeatherSpark's climate averages for Cairo give daytime highs of about 20°C around 20 December and lows of about 11°C, with roughly a two percent chance of a wet day. Sunrise on 21 December is about 06:46 and sunset about 16:59, a little over ten hours of daylight. The group lands at 06:15, before sunrise, so the first hours are cool and grey. The lanes of the quarter are narrow and shaded; stone underfoot can stay cold and slightly damp in the morning. A light jacket for the first two hours, then layers off.
## What to look for, and where to stand

Point out five things. First, at street level near the Mar Girgis metro station, the excavated base of the Roman round tower: stand at the railing and look down to show how far the ground has risen. The round Greek Orthodox church of St George, beside it, is commonly described as standing on the other tower (verify the detail with the guide). Second, from the lane beneath the Hanging Church, look up: the nave is carried over the old southern bastions of the fortress gate, so you are standing in the Roman gateway under a church. Third, the staircase down into the Coptic lane: count the steps aloud as a measure of nineteen centuries of debris. Fourth, if the guide's route allows a glimpse west, Roda's southern tip, where the Nilometer stands, the gauge that once set Egypt's taxes by the river's height. Fifth, the minaret of the Mosque of Amr to the north-east, marking where the Arab camp stood during the siege of the fortress.
stories.why: For the pilgrim, the descent into a sunken quarter turns an abstract date into a physical one: the first-century world is literally below them. For the pastor, the canal-and-toll-gate setting gives an honest way to explain why a refuge tradition settled here (it was a crossroads where travellers stopped) without overclaiming the cave. It also lets him manage expectations about the crypt before anyone is disappointed.
questions: If the Roman city lies several metres down, what does that suggest about how much of the biblical world the group will actually see on this trip?
How would you explain to the group why a refuge tradition might attach to a crossroads rather than a hiding place?
Where on the staircase down will you stop the group to make the point about rising ground, and how long can you afford there?

stories.headline: How a Roman fort became the seed of Cairo
stories.dek: A seven-month siege, a church built over a gate, two rival restorations of a synagogue and a papal blessing explain why the Holy Family's memory sits where it does.
body: The Abu Sirga note already lays out the stratigraphy under that one church, and the Ben Ezra note covers the Geniza, the sale of the building and the Ibn Ezra confusion. This part steps back to the quarter as a whole and to four moments that shaped what the group will see: the siege that made Cairo, the move of the Coptic patriarch, the restoration fights over Ben Ezra, and the twentieth-century internationalising of the Holy Family route. It ends with the sources for the Egypt sojourn itself, which are thinner than most pilgrims assume.
## The siege that made a capital

In 640 the Byzantine garrison in Babylon faced the Arab army of 'Amr ibn al-'As. The fortress held out for about seven months before it fell in December 640 (Wikipedia's Babylon Fortress article; ARCE gives 641 for the conquest as a whole, which includes the later surrender of Alexandria). 'Amr's camp beside the walls became Fustat, the first Muslim capital of Egypt. The later city of Cairo grew north of it. The practical point for the group is that the Christian quarter they walk through is not a Christian enclave that survived inside an Islamic city. It is the original core, and the Islamic city grew up around it.

That reversal explains the quarter's compression. Churches, a synagogue and later a mosque are all within a short walk of each other because the old fortress walls fixed the space, and the Arab city spread outside them.
## The church that hangs

The Hanging Church (al-Mu'allaqa), dedicated to the Virgin, is the quarter's best-known building, and its history is separate from Abu Sirga's. Its nave is carried over a passage on the southern bastions that marked the fortress's main gate, hence the name. The church's earliest written mention comes in the biography of Patriarch Joseph I (831–849), and it was probably built during the patriarchate of Isaac, with an earlier building possibly behind it. In 1047, during the tenure of Pope Christodoulos, the patriarchal residence moved from Alexandria to Cairo, and the Hanging Church became its official seat (Wikipedia, Hanging Church; ARCE also dates the move to 1047). The building was damaged in 1983 and again in the 1992 earthquake; restoration was completed in 2011.

For a guide's narrative, the line of succession is useful: Abu Sirga hosted early episcopal business (see the Abu Sirga note's reception table), but from the eleventh century the Hanging Church was where the head of the Coptic Church lived. The group will pass through both, and they are not the same story.
## Two restorations of one synagogue

Ben Ezra has been restored twice in living memory, and the two restorations have competing stories. From 1980 to 1991 the Montreal architect and philanthropist Phyllis Lambert led and funded a restoration of the synagogue, documented in the 1994 volume she edited, Fortifications and the Synagogue: The Fortress of Babylon and the Ben Ezra Synagogue, Cairo (Jerusalem Post). Much later the Egyptian state carried out its own restoration, presented by the antiquities minister Ahmed Issa as ceiling reinforcement, insulation, new lighting and cleaning of the marble columns, and inaugurated by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly. The Jerusalem Post reported that the official account omitted Lambert's eleven years of work and that none of Egypt's remaining Jews were invited to the unveiling.

Why mention this on a pilgrimage? Because it is a clean example of how heritage sites are narrated by whoever holds them. The same is true at Christian sites the group will visit: the story you hear at the door is the custodian's story. That is not a reason for cynicism, only for asking who is telling it.
## The route goes international

The Abu Sirga note records Egypt's 2000 decision to treat the Holy Family route as national heritage. The Catholic Church added its weight later. On 4 October 2017, at a Wednesday general audience in St Peter's Square, Pope Francis greeted an Egyptian delegation led by Tourism Minister Yahya Rashed, which had come to promote the route, and blessed an icon of the Flight into Egypt (Vatican Radio). The route as promoted then has eight stations, beginning at Al-Arish in North Sinai and running through the eastern delta to Wadi al-Natrun. One irony is worth noting for safety reasons later: the route's first station lies in North Sinai, where the UK Foreign Office advises against all travel.
## What the sources actually say

Matthew is the only first-century witness to the sojourn, and he names no town in Egypt and no length of stay; he says only that the family remained until Herod's death (Matt 2:15). Everything else comes later and in three streams. The Coptic tradition rests mainly on the vision attributed to Patriarch Theophilus (covered in the Abu Sirga note). A Latin stream, the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, usually dated to around the early seventh century (NASSCAL's e-Clavis entry summarises the dating debate), tells how the idols of a temple in the Egyptian city of Sotinen fell when Mary and the child entered, and how the governor, Affrodosius, came and worshipped. An Arabic infancy tradition adds more miracle stories. None of these is history in the modern sense, and none was meant to be.

The fair way to present Old Cairo, then, uses the classification from Day 1. The Nile and the fortress are geography. The Holy Family's presence in Egypt is canonical but unlocated. The cave at Abu Sirga is a commemoration, kept for over fifteen centuries by a church that has its own reasons to remember a refugee Christ. Saying this plainly does not diminish the place; it lets pilgrims honour it for what it is.
stories.why: Knowing that the quarter is Cairo's original core changes how the group sees the Copts: not as a remnant but as the oldest residents. For the pastor, the contrast between Matthew's silence and the later stories is a ready-made lesson in how Scripture differs from tradition, delivered at a site where both are on display. The Ben Ezra restoration dispute is a small warning to listen for who is telling each site's story.
questions: If Matthew deliberately leaves the Egyptian sojourn unlocated, what does that suggest about what he wanted readers to take from it?
How would you explain to a pilgrim the difference between Pseudo-Matthew's falling idols and the canonical account without sounding dismissive of Coptic piety?
Where else on this trip will the group hear a custodian's account of a site, and how will you help them weigh it?

stories.headline: Egypt had a Jewish temple when Jesus arrived
stories.dek: The Holy Family fled into a Roman province outside Herod's reach, where Jewish soldiers had kept a temple for two centuries; today the group meets Copts at prayer and a synagogue with almost no Jews left.
body: Two worlds meet on Day 2. One is the Egypt that a Judean family on the run would have entered around 4 BC. The other is the Egypt of December 2026: a Coptic church in its most musical month and a Jewish community reduced to a handful of elderly women. Both deserve more than a photo stop.
## Why Egypt was a refuge at all

The point is political before it is pious. Since 30 BC Egypt had been a Roman province governed by a prefect answering to Augustus, not part of Herod's client kingdom. Herod's authority stopped at the border. A family crossing into Egypt passed beyond the reach of his soldiers in a way that a family hiding in Galilee or Transjordan would not. Matthew's angel gives no reason, but anyone in the first century would have understood the logic: you flee across a jurisdiction line. That is what refugees still do. (The Matthew 2:13–15 Theology Note treats the Greek verb for flight; this part stays with the map.)
## A second temple by the Nile

The Abu Sirga and Ben Ezra notes mention Jewish Egypt through Elephantine, Alexandria and the Septuagint. One institution is missing from them, and it is the most surprising. When the Holy Family arrived, a Jewish temple with priests and sacrifices was operating in Egypt, about 25 kilometres north of Cairo, at the site now called Tell el-Yahudiyeh (the Mound of the Jewess), near ancient Leontopolis in the district of Heliopolis.

According to Josephus, a priest named Onias (sources disagree whether Onias III or his son Onias IV; the Jewish Virtual Library favours IV) fled the turmoil in Jerusalem in the 170s–160s BC and asked Ptolemy VI and Cleopatra II for permission to build a temple. Josephus says Onias appealed to Isaiah 19:19, the promise of an altar to the LORD in the midst of Egypt. The settlers around it were largely military colonists in Ptolemaic service; two of Onias's sons later served as generals for Cleopatra III. The temple stood until 73 AD, when Vespasian, fearing it could become a centre of revolt after the Jewish war, ordered the prefect Tiberius Julius Lupus to close it; Lupus died during the process and his successor Paulinus completed the stripping (Wikipedia, Land of Onias; Jewish Virtual Library).

The rabbis treated it with a careful mixture of disapproval and recognition. The Mishnah (Menahot 13:10) allows certain vows made for Jerusalem to be fulfilled there, but says a priest who served at Onias's altar could not serve in Jerusalem. The Talmud calls the temple forbidden, but not idolatry.

What should a pilgrim make of this? Nothing in Matthew connects the Holy Family to Leontopolis, and any suggestion that they visited it is pure hypothesis. But it changes the picture of what Joseph walked into. Egypt was not simply pagan territory; it held a large, organised Jewish world with its own sanctuary, soldiers and synagogues. A displaced Judean family with a trade (Matthew 13:55 calls Joseph a tektōn, a builder or craftsman) could plausibly look for work and shelter among people who shared its law and language. That too is hypothesis, but it is the kind that fits the first century.
## The Copts in the month of praise

On 20 December the Coptic calendar is in the month of Kiahk, which Copts devote to praises of the Virgin and the Incarnation in the weeks before their Christmas. The long night praise services (the Tasbeha) are especially loved in this month and often run through Saturday night into Sunday morning. The group arrives in Old Cairo on a Sunday morning; it is very likely that a liturgy will be under way or just ending in at least one of the churches. (Day 1 covered the Nativity Fast and the 7 January Christmas; this is about the Sunday the group will actually be present.)

That means the group may be walking past worshippers, not tourists. Coptic liturgy is long, sung largely in Coptic and Arabic, and accompanied by cymbals and triangle. Pilgrims who stand quietly at the back for even five minutes will hear something very old.
## A synagogue without a congregation

Ben Ezra is no longer a functioning synagogue (Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities site says so plainly). Egypt had about 80,000 Jews when Israel was founded in 1948. In 2019 the Times of Israel (JTA) reported that the death of the matriarch Marcelle Haroun left five Jews known to be living in Cairo, all women of one family led by her daughter Magda Haroun, who heads the community. A later Jerusalem Post report counted six in Cairo and a few dozen in Alexandria. The group is visiting the memorial of a community that is almost gone, inside a quarter where the Christians who host it are themselves a minority.
## How the group should behave

First, if a liturgy is in progress, stand at the back, do not walk across the nave, do not photograph worshippers' faces, and keep children and phones silent. Women may wish to cover their heads in Coptic churches; bring a scarf rather than be asked. Do not step onto the raised sanctuary behind the icon screen. Second, at Ben Ezra, treat the building as a Jewish holy place, not a Christian prop: no group prayers, songs or devotional readings inside. Do the reading outside afterwards. Third, follow Egypt's general photography rules (UK Foreign Office): ask before photographing Egyptians, never photograph children, police, military or government buildings. Fourth, buy something small from a Coptic vendor in the lanes: a cross, a candle, a book. It is an act of fellowship, not just shopping.
stories.why: Seeing Egypt as a refuge across a border, and as a land with its own Jewish temple, keeps the Holy Family story concrete rather than sentimental. For the pastor, the Kiahk Sunday is a chance to show the group a living ancient church at worship, and the near-empty synagogue is a sober reminder of what happens to communities when the neighbours stop protecting them. Both shape how the group carries itself in the lanes.
questions: How does knowing that Herod's power stopped at the Egyptian border change the way you read the angel's command?
What does the Temple of Onias, justified by Isaiah 19:19, tell you about how Jews in Egypt read the prophets about their adopted land?
How will you brief the group to behave if they arrive at Abu Sirga in the middle of the Sunday liturgy?

stories.headline: Matthew read all of Hosea 11, not one verse
stories.dek: Hosea already expected a second exodus out of Egypt, and Isaiah promised that Egypt itself would be called God's people, so the flight to Egypt opens a door wider than the escape.
body: Hermeneutical lens: Canonical-Intertextual. The texts are Matthew 2:13–15 with Hosea 11:1–11 (read whole) and Isaiah 19:19–25.

The Matthew 2:13–15 Theology Note already covers the verb for flight, the fulfilment formula, "my son" against the Greek "his children", the dreams, the Joseph typology and displacement as God's method. This edition asks two other questions. Did Matthew tear Hosea 11:1 out of context? And what does the canon say about Egypt itself?
## The context problem

Hosea 11:1 looks backwards. God loved Israel as a child, and "out of Egypt I called my son" describes the exodus of the nation centuries earlier. It is not, on its face, a prediction, and many readers conclude Matthew borrowed words that sounded right. G. K. Beale's 2012 article in the Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society answers from the whole chapter.

Beale shows that Hosea 11 tells a story in four movements: the past exodus (v. 1), Israel's ingratitude and idolatry (vv. 2–5), judgment held back by divine compassion (vv. 6–9), and a future restoration (vv. 10–11).
## Hosea's own second exodus

The future movement is explicit. In verses 10–11 the LORD roars like a lion, and his children come trembling from the west; they come "like birds from Egypt, and like doves from the land of Assyria". The Hebrew is vivid: yeḥerdû kəṣippôr mimmiṣrayim, they will flutter like a bird out of Egypt. Beale notes that Hosea 1:10–11 and 11:11 are the only Old Testament texts that explicitly promise a future return from Egypt. So when Hosea wrote "out of Egypt I called my son", he already expected the pattern to be repeated: God had called his son out of Egypt once and would do it again at the end.

Beale also hears an echo behind the lion. The only places in the Old Testament that combine "out of Egypt" with a lion comparison are Balaam's oracles (Numbers 23:22, 24; 24:8–9) and Hosea 11:10–11. In the Greek of Numbers 24:7–8 the one God brings out of Egypt is a single royal figure, a man from Israel's seed who will rule many nations. Beale calls this an echo, not a direct allusion. It matters for Matthew because the same oracles supply the star of Numbers 24:17 behind the magi (Matt 2:2): a king's star, and a king brought out of Egypt.
Matthew did not find a hidden prediction; he read Hosea's pattern of exodus, exile and greater exodus and saw its decisive instance in Jesus.
## Why the quotation comes on the way in

A further puzzle: Matthew quotes "out of Egypt I called my son" in 2:15, when the family is entering Egypt, not in 2:21, when they leave. Beale gives two reasons. First, verse 15 already says they remained "until the death of Herod", so the quotation looks ahead to the return. Second, Hosea's own storyline has the same shape: out of Egypt (11:1), back toward Egypt (11:5), out again (11:11). The descent is part of the pattern, not an interruption of it.

Verse 5 carries a textual crux worth knowing. The Hebrew begins lōʾ yāšûb, "he shall not return to the land of Egypt" (ESV), but many interpreters take the first word as an assertion or a question, which yields "they will return to Egypt" or "will they not return to Egypt?" (NIV). Beale reads it as a real return. Either way, Egypt in Hosea is both house of bondage and the place Israel drifts back to.
Beale rejects reading Egypt as a code word for Herod's Israel: Matthew uses "Egypt" literally in 2:13, 14 and 19.
## Blessed be Egypt my people

The Ben Ezra note lists Isaiah 19:18–25 in one line; it is the canon's most astonishing word about Egypt. In 19:19–20 the prophet promises an altar to the LORD in the midst of Egypt and a pillar at its border. Then he reverses the exodus. Egypt will cry to the LORD because of oppressors, and the LORD will send them a saviour (môšîaʿ) who will deliver them. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of Exodus 2–3, when Israel cried out under Pharaoh. Now the oppressor nation is the one crying, and God answers it.

Then comes verse 25: "Blessed be Egypt my people" (ʿammî), with Assyria called the work of God's hands and Israel his inheritance. Three titles that belong to Israel are shared out among Israel's two great oppressors. The Greek translators in Alexandria seem to have found this too much: the Septuagint renders it as a blessing on "my people who are in Egypt", that is, the Jewish diaspora. The Hebrew does not narrow it.
## The Christological centre

Jesus is the Son who goes down into Egypt as Israel did, and the one through whom Hosea's greater exodus begins. But the canon also promises that Egypt itself will be called "my people". The church that keeps the cave at Abu Sirga is part of the answer to that promise: Egyptians were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and Coptic Christianity grew from them. The child who took refuge in Egypt is the saviour Isaiah said God would send to Egypt.
## From text to practice

Three practices follow from what God has already done. Read Hosea 11:1–11 aloud on the bus, so the group hears the story Matthew heard. At Abu Sirga, after seeing the Copts at worship, pray Isaiah 19:25 over them: a confession of what God has already said. And let pilgrims name their own Egypts, and hear that the Son has been there and the way out runs through him.
stories.why: Pilgrims who have heard that Matthew misused the Old Testament get a calm, text-based answer on Egyptian soil. Isaiah 19 lets the group see Egypt as a nation God promised to call his own, turning the meeting with the Coptic church into recognition. It keeps the devotion Christ-centred rather than a lesson in resilience.
questions: How does reading Hosea 11:10–11 change what you hear in 11:1?
What would it mean for this group to pray "Blessed be Egypt my people" sincerely while standing among Egyptian Christians?
If Matthew saw Balaam's oracles behind both the star and the exodus, what kind of king is he presenting in chapter 2?
stories.counterpoint: The strongest alternative holds that Matthew did not read Hosea in context at all. Richard Longenecker's Biblical Exegesis in the Apostolic Period argues that the apostles used the Jewish, pesher-like methods of their day, which Christians may admire but should not imitate; Matthew's use of Hosea is inspired but not a model for preachers. Beale's whole-chapter reading answers this on its own ground, but serious scholars still hold it.

source.outlet: Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society
source.title: The Use of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15: One More Time
source.author: G. K. Beale

stories.headline: Sleepless pilgrims, a Sunday liturgy and sunken lanes
stories.dek: Day 2 starts at 06:15 after a night in transit, so the brief is about pacing tired legs on old stairs, timing the visit around Coptic worship and getting the money and papers right on the first morning.
body: Day 2 is the easiest site day and the riskiest TL day of the Egypt leg, because everyone arrives exhausted after the 04:00 Dubai connection (EK929). Old Cairo is compact but full of steps, uneven stone and dark interiors. The aim is modest: immigration, two sites seen well, food, and the hotel with nobody hurt and nothing lost.
## How the day runs

A proposal; confirm with the Egypt guide. 06:15 land. Per the Prep Hub: gather, toilets, completeness check, arrival cards and visa barcodes from the airport assistant, immigration, baggage, hand over to the guide. Allow 60 to 90 minutes (estimate). Then breakfast, ideally at the hotel if Panorama can secure an early check-in or day room.

Ben Ezra opens 09:00 to 16:00 (Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities), so arrive about 09:30: Roman tower, Hanging Church (29 steps up), Ben Ezra, then Abu Sirga last, when the Sunday liturgy is more likely to have ended (hypothesis; ask the guide). Allow two and a half to three hours. Walking is well under a kilometre (estimate), but there are stairs at the entrance, the Hanging Church and the Abu Sirga crypt, which may be closed.

For elderly pilgrims the stairs, not the distance, are the issue: decide before landing who skips the Hanging Church stairs and the crypt, and seat them in a courtyard with a buddy. Toilets are few; use the hotel or restaurant first. Lanes are shaded, rain unlikely, mornings cool.
## Dress, rules and crowds

Shoulders and knees covered; a scarf for women in Coptic churches. No flash. Photography inside Ben Ezra is widely reported to be restricted; confirm and obey the attendant. Never photograph worshippers' faces or step behind the icon screen. The UK Foreign Office notes that photographing military sites, police, government buildings or children is prohibited and that drones need Defence Ministry permission: no drones in Egypt.

Expect a busy Sunday: Coptic families leaving Kiahk liturgy, plus December tour groups clustering mid-morning. The lanes are narrow and look alike. Agree the exact pick-up point with the driver before anyone leaves the bus.
## Counts, safety and papers
Count five times: airport kerb; bus drop; top of the stairs into the lanes; courtyard outside Ben Ezra; on the bus before leaving. Every elderly pilgrim gets a named buddy for the day.

The UK Foreign Office page (updated 27 October 2026, still current when checked 25 November 2026) adds regional-tension warnings and says terrorists are likely to try to attack in Egypt, including religious sites and gatherings. No Cairo-specific restriction; avoid demonstrations. North Sinai, where the Holy Family route starts at Al-Arish, is advised against entirely; the group's Sinai days are in the south.

Passports need six months' validity. For British passports the visa on arrival is US$30 cash, or since 1 August 2026 a digital one at Cairo for US$36 by card; confirm with Panorama what Indonesian passports need (the Prep Hub's visa barcodes suggest it is pre-arranged). Egyptian pounds are capped at EGP 5,000 in or out.
## Money and the bus briefing

The rate on 24 November 2026 was about EGP 54.2 to the US dollar (Amwal Al Ghad, six-bank average). Change a modest amount at the airport in 10, 20 and 50 pound notes for toilets and small buys. Hawkers near the entrance: a smiling no-thank-you while walking. Take numbers and cash for the optional Nile dinner cruise on the morning bus, not at 17:00.

Bus script: "Welcome to Egypt. You have not slept, so today we go slowly. Three things. Stairs: Old Cairo lies below today's street. Hold the rail, and if you would rather wait in a courtyard, tell Tesa now. Worship: it is Sunday, and the Copts may be at prayer. If we walk into a service, we stand at the back, silent, no photos of faces. Buddies: these lanes all look alike. If lost, stand still and WhatsApp me. Today we stand where tradition says Jesus was a refugee. Now I will read you the whole of Hosea 11. Listen for Egypt."
## Handover and what goes wrong

No service is scheduled, but in the courtyard outside Abu Sirga, away from any liturgy, Merrick reads Hosea 11:10–11 and prays Isaiah 19:25 over the Coptic church; five minutes. Tesa takes the count and the guide's clock. Merrick's TL load peaks at the airport, so no spiritual input before the bus.

Common failures: a tired pilgrim misses a step (TL in front, Tesa behind on every stair); someone drifts into a side lane (buddies, counts); passports left on the bus (the bus is not a safe); only large notes (small-notes rule); disappointment at a closed crypt (set expectations on the bus).
## Fun facts

1. Amr ibn al-As told the caliph Umar that a Nile rise of 16 cubits on the Roda gauge meant an abundant harvest, while 18 would flood a quarter of Egypt and usually bring plague (Wikipedia, Nilometer).
2. When Ahmad ibn Tulun restored the Roda Nilometer in 872–873, he removed the name of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil from its inscription (Wikipedia, Nilometer).
3. Josephus says the Jewish temple at Leontopolis stood for 343 years, but scholars think he slipped and meant about 243 (Wikipedia, Land of Onias; Jewish Virtual Library).
4. Flinders Petrie made a model of what he believed was the Onias temple and showed it to London's Jewish community in 1906; the model has since disappeared (Jewish Virtual Library).
5. The Hanging Church holds about 110 icons, the oldest from the eighth century (Wikipedia, Hanging Church).
6. Ten carved wooden door panels from the Hanging Church are now in the British Museum (Wikipedia, Hanging Church).

7. The Coptic Museum in the same quarter opened in 1910 thanks to Marcus Simaika Pasha, who bought architectural pieces from churches being renovated; foreign adults pay EGP 280 (Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities).
stories.why: The first morning sets the pattern for the trip. If counts, buddies and stair discipline work on a sleepless day in Cairo, they will work at Petra. For the pastor, separating the airport (TL hat) from the courtyard devotion (pastor hat) protects the one spiritual moment of the day from logistics.
questions: Which pilgrims will skip the stairs and the crypt, and who will sit with them?
Has Panorama confirmed exactly what Indonesian passports need on arrival and whether the visa is prepaid?
Where exactly will the bus pick the group up after Abu Sirga, and has the driver confirmed it?
